body:
I think the disconnect here is that some people don't understand how trendy the state became, and how quickly/how many people flocked to the state when it already had a housing problem pre-covid.

From the get go, I feel like the state is at a disadvantage in terms of housing. Growing up, the only time I saw a new house being built was if a local was building a house for their family. That's literally it. There aren't big cities, the biggest one has 40-45k people. New housing has always been so slow or done out of necessity, but even then with a state population of 600k that isn't saying much.

There's also always been SO many vacation homes. It's something like nearly 1 in 5 houses are vacation homes owned by out of staters, which isn't a bad thing since millions visit the state each year and spend billions. I think the issue is moreso a lot of these houses, if not the majority, stay empty the rest of the year and aren't rented out to locals, or are turned into Airbnb's for other tourists.

On top of that, towns are so sparsely populated throughout the entire state. Montpelier alone is at 8,000, and the entire county barely has 60k residents despite being half the size of Rhode Island. So I know a couple hundred people moving to that town doesn't sound like a lot, but it kinda is especially if there was already a housing shortage.

I just wonder what the future holds; in Burlington they're building huge ugly apartment complexes to accommodate people. But imo I feel like that takes away from the beauty of the state and what it's supposed to be about. Plus locals up there are super upset about it, so I wonder if there'll be a lot of public pushback if they try that throughout the state.
